prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After reading the full exchange and the chair's questions, my reasons are the same but better tested. First, the originating idea is specific and traceable: a lattice at the magic wavelength makes the light shift on the clock transition cancel while the atoms are held motionless, so many atoms can be interrogated without Doppler and recoil shifts. Second, Ye's group, with the cavity-stabilised laser and the many-body and spin-exchange control developed in that programme, then carried the performance to roughly 1e-18, and that is the part that turned a proposal into a standard. Third, the chair's summary records that no member raises a reproducibility or maturity doubt, and the figures have been compared across several national and university laboratories. As to the chair's first question on scope, I would frame the prize as an invention that is already producing physics and not as a general measurement capability: the 2005 prize was for the frequency comb and for laser-based precision spectroscopy, the 2012 prize was for methods to measure and control individual quantum systems including ion clocks, and the lattice clock is the first design in which a large ensemble of neutral atoms, with its many-body shifts, reaches that accuracy. Constraints on constants and gravitational redshift resolved across millimetre scales are results already in hand, not only promises. I therefore think a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself, and not precision spectroscopy in general, separates it adequately from both earlier prizes.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one nearly everyone listed: this is a measurement invention, and the largest consequences named in the case, the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and drift or dark-matter searches, are still mostly prospective. If the committee holds that the Prize should go to a new phenomenon or a new state of matter, then twisted bilayer graphene is the stronger claim in kind, and I would not call the clock the uniquely correct choice. The second reservation is credit. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill contributed to the early strontium demonstrations and to the stability record, and a two-name prize cannot capture them; I see this as a real cost that the citation should not hide by overclaiming. Third, I rely on recalled 1e-18 figures and on the chronology of the first lattice clocks, and I am not an atomic-physics specialist, so I defer to colleagues who can judge the polarisability and blackbody-shift budget.

responses.point: Danielsson is the only member whose preferred configuration is magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B022) with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, and he argues that the prediction-then-observation structure is the pattern the committee should favour over a measurement capability.
responses.response: I have the most sympathy for this position, as a theorist working on correlated electrons and magnetism. The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed seven years later by the 2018 observation is exactly the structure I would like to reward, and I agree the phenomenology is secure and reproduced widely. My difference is about timing and what a citation could honestly say. Eight years after the experiment, the pairing mechanism, the phase diagram and the dependence on twist angle and sample disorder are not settled, and a citation would have to be worded around phenomena and not around understanding. The experimental credit is also spread over Cao, Fatemi, and the groups of Dean, Young and Kim, which no three names can represent. I would not call B022 premature and I now carry it as my first alternative, but where he sees a discovery-versus-capability question I see maturity and attribution tipping the balance for this cycle.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B025 but asks the committee to state clearly what is new relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, to verify the 1e-18 figures and chronology against primary intercomparisons, and to acknowledge the early strontium contributors.
responses.response: I agree with all three requests and think they belong in the committee's record. On scope, my answer above is that the ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice is the distinct step, not the comb and not single-ion control. On verification, I accept that before the citation is fixed the uncertainty figures and the order of the first lattice-clock demonstrations should be checked against primary papers, since I and several others quote them from memory. On credit I would go slightly further than the chair's summary: the deliberation should name Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley as contributors, while the citation stays tied to the concept and to the record performance. I also note, with respect, that she has set aside her own first-place B008 on field-proximity grounds, which I think is the right call, and I have done the same with my own field's B029.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock rests on demanding atomic structure (polarisabilities, blackbody and higher-order light shifts) and that the clocks feed back into fundamental physics, and she wants the citation worded around the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself and the contributions of Lemonde and the ion-clock lineage acknowledged.
responses.response: Her answer is the one that most reduces my concern about discovery versus instrument. If the accuracy claim is only meaningful because the atomic-structure calculations are understood at the 1e-18 level, then this is physics resting on controlled theory, a point I cannot judge myself and am glad she can. I accept her wording suggestion and have used it in my citation. I disagree only slightly on timing: she notes the second has not been redefined, but I do not think the Prize should wait for an administrative decision by the metrology community. The relevant evidence is the cross-laboratory agreement that already exists, and a redefinition would then be a consequence of the invention and not a condition for rewarding it.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, now puts the lattice clock first but describes it as a measurement capability, not a discovery of new phenomena, and keeps IceCube (B007) as an alternative because it opens a new observational window.
responses.response: I take his framing of the clock as a capability seriously, and I do not dispute that the neutrino window is a discovery in the plain sense. I place IceCube lower for reasons he partly shares: the diffuse flux is firm, but source identification rests on a single blazar association at about three sigma plus Galactic-plane evidence, and the credit within a long lineage from DUMAND and Baikal through AMANDA is hard to settle with two names. I cannot judge the instrumental claims as an astroparticle specialist and would defer to him and Kroll on that. For this cycle, a clean two-name configuration whose results are already intercompared seems to me more defensible than a stronger window that is still being resolved.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how the citation is scoped.
How heavily the claims of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill should weigh against a two-name credit, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
Whether the 1e-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks, which I quote from memory, hold up against the primary intercomparisons.
Whether a later thorium nuclear-clock decision would sit uneasily with crediting Ye now; I regard that technology as too immature to compete this year.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or any credited name on the shortlist, and the preferred configuration does not lie in my research area, so I see no reason to recuse myself on B025. My profile documents professional proximity to electronic-structure theory and magnetism, hence to B029, B036 and B022, which I have tried not to overweight; I note that I regard the proximity disclosed by Olsson, Kroll and Johansson as a matter for them and the chair to judge. I have nothing new to disclose since round 1.
